title: First the row, then the audience
hook: anyone who comes to see the Guru eats first in langar; tradition says the emperor Akbar sat on the floor too

segments.voice: Yesterday: the baoli, eighty-four steps down to shared water. Water for all.

Meeting someone important usually works the same way. A waiting room, a line, a list, and someone at a desk deciding who goes first. The more important the visitor, the shorter the wait. At Goindval, visiting Guru Amar Das worked differently. Before anyone at all could sit with the Guru, they first had to sit on the floor in the langar, the community kitchen, in a row with everyone else, and eat. Farmers, merchants, beggars, priests. And one day, tradition says, the Mughal emperor himself came to Goindval: Akbar.
screen: `WAITING ROOMS AND GUEST LISTS.` → `AT GOINDVAL, EVERYONE EATS FIRST.` → `THEN THE EMPEROR ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: Sikhs sum up the rule in a short Punjabi saying: pehlan pangat, pichhon sangat. First the row, then the gathering. The pangat is the row of people sitting side by side on the floor to eat; the sangat is the gathering around the Guru. The order matters. You don't get to the Guru until you've eaten as an equal with everyone else. Tradition says Akbar honored the rule. The emperor sat down on the floor in the row, among ordinary people, and ate the simple food of the kitchen before he met Guru Amar Das. Some tellings add that he was so moved he offered the Guru a grant of land, and the Guru declined it, saying the kitchen should be supported by the community's own work and giving, not by a king. Historians note that the visit comes to us through Sikh tradition, and the details vary. But the rule itself is still kept today. Yesterday it was water; today it's food. A shared meal says who counts as your equal, and in that world rules of rank and caste said who could sit and eat with whom. The pangat wipes that line out, on the floor, every day. Nobody sits at the head. Nobody gets a higher seat. The same food, from the same pot, served by volunteers. Guru Nanak had begun the langar, and Mata Khivi had kept it going. Guru Amar Das made it the doorway. Before you meet the Guru, you meet your neighbor, at eye level, on the floor.
screen: `PEHLAN PANGAT, PICHHON SANGAT.` · `PANGAT — THE ROW ON THE FLOOR.` · `THE EMPEROR SAT IN THE ROW.` · `NOBODY AT THE HEAD.` · then, large: `FIRST THE ROW.`

segments.voice: Picture the row: faces side by side, all at the same height. At your next meal, sit where you usually don't, and let someone else be served first, or serve everyone yourself and sit down last. If you eat alone, eat on the floor or at a counter, somewhere without a head of the table.
Pangat. The row where everyone, even an emperor, sat on the floor at Goindval and ate as equals before meeting the Guru.
Your line: nobody sits at the head. Tomorrow, the preachers, women and men. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: In gurdwaras, langar is served to anyone who comes, seated together in rows on the floor, in pangat; the saying pehlan pangat, pichhon sangat is often quoted to explain why.
